stories.headline: House Heads Toward Vote on Impeaching Hegseth as Congress Returns
stories.dek: Trump defends the defense secretary while Democrats and Rep. Thomas Massie push impeachment over the Iran war.
pole_a_bullets: Impeachment is meant for high crimes, not for disagreement over a war the commander-in-chief ordered.
Hegseth carried out the president's Iran strategy, and Trump says he is being punished for winning.
The push is political payback by Democrats and a defeated congressman, and Hegseth calls the articles a sham.
A lame-duck session with a funding deadline and a defense bill should not be consumed by a symbolic vote.
pole_b_bullets: Jeffries accuses Hegseth of abusing his authority and compromising national security.
Congress has a duty to hold a cabinet officer accountable for a costly war with Iran.
The effort is not purely partisan: a Republican, Massie, wrote the resolution, and other Republicans have signaled support.
House Republican leaders blocked a vote in September, so a vote now restores normal oversight.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions voiced by President Trump, Defense Secretary Hegseth and Republican allies.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions voiced by House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and other Democrats.
evidence_left: Jeffries said Sunday on ABC that he is a "hard yes" on the Hegseth resolution (reported by U.S. News and ANI).
Massie tabled the resolution in September. Speaker Mike Johnson sent the House home early to stop a vote (NBC News, U.S. News).
evidence_right: Trump defended Hegseth to reporters Sunday night (U.S. News). NBC reports passage would need all Democrats plus several Republicans.
CNN reports Massie plans to trigger a vote this week. U.S. News says a number of Republicans have signaled they could join Democrats.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CNN, U.S. News & World Report, NBC News, ANI, November 09, 2026.

stories.headline: Trump Says Deportations 'Might Be Too Tough' Days After Promoting Stephen Miller
stories.dek: The president floated an immigration deal with Democrats while elevating the architect of the crackdown to chief of staff.
pole_a_bullets: Trump's remark was aimed at long-settled, law-abiding workers, not at enforcement as a whole.
Trump said immigration "both helped and hurt" and named Iran and messaging as the main causes of the losses.
Miller's promotion shows the enforcement agenda stays in place, and he gives hardliners a seat at the table.
Any deal with Democrats would be negotiated from the White House, with border security as the price.
pole_b_bullets: Trump's admission confirms what critics said: the raids went too far and cost the GOP at the polls.
Promoting Miller hours before the interview aired contradicts any promise to soften policy.
There is no sign the administration is considering concrete changes, so Democrats should not trade on words alone.
Democrats will control both chambers and can set the terms of any immigration talks.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by Trump allies and immigration-enforcement advocates.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by congressional Democrats and immigrant-rights advocates.
evidence_left: In the 60 Minutes interview, Trump said "I think it might be too tough," citing immigrants who had lived in the U.S. for 10+ years without serious crimes (CNN).
The interview was recorded Friday, the day Trump named Miller to replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff (Local 12/Scripps).
evidence_right: A Fox News midterm poll found 58% of voters said Trump's immigration enforcement went too far. About 60% disapproved of ICE's job performance (as reported by The Daily Wire).
CNN reports it is unclear whether Trump is considering changes to his immigration agenda.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CNN, Local 12 / Scripps News, Newsweek, The Daily Wire, November 09, 2026.

stories.headline: Democratic Midterm Wins Put AI Rules and Data Centers in Play
stories.dek: Democrats plan AI testing, liability and data-center bills for January after a tech sell-off tied to regulation fears.
pole_a_bullets: Data-center moratoriums and pre-release audits could slow the AI buildout that is driving U.S. growth.
Investors are already pricing in the risk. Trajan Wealth's David Busch cited fears of far more regulation and pushback on data centers.
Trump says he will work with states that embrace AI and opposes mandatory federal constraints, to keep the U.S. ahead of China.
Rules should be set with industry input, and no AI law has actually passed yet. Premature restrictions would cost jobs and investment.
pole_b_bullets: Democrats want to shield consumers from electricity costs linked to data centers.
Rep. Lori Trahan wants independent experts to evaluate leading models against safety standards before release.
Companies should face clear liability when AI systems cause harm, and executives should testify under oath, per Rep. Greg Casar.
Warnings that AI could escape human control justify guardrails, and Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed called for an independent AI agency.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by the Trump administration, AI-industry backers and market analysts.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by incoming Democratic lawmakers and AI-safety advocates.
evidence_left: Bloomberg reports Citi strategists cut U.S. stocks after the S&P 500's biggest weekly loss since April 2025. It reports $2.3 trillion was wiped off the Nasdaq 100 on Thursday alone.

Tech-Insider, citing Deutsche Welle, reports more than $2.5 trillion was lost globally and the Nasdaq fell 5.52% in the week. That is a different measure from Bloomberg's, and the Tech-Insider write-up is a single secondary source.
evidence_right: Reuters reports Democrats plan bills on data-center electricity costs, independent testing of advanced AI and liability for AI-caused harm (via The Business Standard).
Tech-Insider notes no new AI law has passed. NBC Montana reports the legislative path is unclear because the parties are divided on approach.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from Reuters via The Business Standard, Bloomberg via Yahoo Finance, NBC Montana, Tech-Insider, November 09, 2026.

stories.headline: Nvidia Board Opens Probe Into CEO Jensen Huang's Ties to Alleged Chinese Spy
stories.dek: Huang apologized for an affair and remains CEO as the stock falls and Beijing denies the allegation.
pole_a_bullets: The board says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised.
Huang stays in place and an independent committee with outside counsel runs the probe, a standard governance response.
The sell-off is about a leadership question, not demand. Other chip stocks mostly rose Monday.
Analyst Dan Ives expects Huang to continue as CEO without near-term interruption.
pole_b_bullets: Key-person risk is large: Ives says Huang could be removed depending on the investigation.
U.S. intelligence reportedly judged the woman, whose company bought Nvidia chips, to be gathering information for Beijing.
Huang has lobbied the administration to ease China chip-sale limits, so the relationship raises conflict-of-interest questions.
House Republicans are demanding answers, so congressional scrutiny could follow.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions voiced by Nvidia's board and spokesperson and by bullish analysts such as Dan Ives.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions voiced by House Republicans, national-security-minded critics and cautious investors.
evidence_left: Nvidia's board announced the investigation Sunday and said Huang will remain CEO during it (KOIN/CNN, CNBC).
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the spy allegation is unsubstantiated (CNBC, citing Reuters; NBC News).
evidence_right: The New York Times reported U.S. intelligence determined the woman was gathering information for Beijing (via KOIN/CNN). NBC cites an unnamed person familiar with the matter.
Nvidia shares fell 5% Monday per CNBC. Yahoo Finance showed a 4.26% drop earlier in the session.
stories.sources_line: Sourced from CNBC, NBC News, Fox Business, KOIN (CNN), November 09, 2026.

stories.headline: Strong Jobs Data Revives December Rate-Hike Debate as Stocks Rebound
stories.dek: October payrolls beat forecasts and inflation data lands Tuesday, with markets still shaken by last week's AI sell-off.
pole_a_bullets: A solid economy gives the Fed room to finish the inflation fight without breaking growth, per SF Fed President Mary Daly.
Hiring is strong: 165,000 jobs against a 65,000 forecast, with unemployment down to 4.1%.
Oxford Economics says falling tech stocks and oil could remove the case for a hike in early 2027.
Stocks are recovering, with the Dow and S&P up Monday, and Brent crude has fallen from over $112 to near $93.
pole_b_bullets: Inflation is the Fed's main concern: September's annual rate was 3.7% and December hike odds are near 80%.
Daly says Americans are on a "treadmill of high inflation" and more hikes are likely.
The AI buildout is pushing up energy and hardware prices, and Fed minutes tied it to September's hike.
Axios flags the worst market day in 18 months as a sign financial conditions may already be tightening. The rebound looks tentative, per Capital.com's Daniela Hathorn.
stories.pole_a_who: Positions commonly voiced by market optimists and some Fed officials.
stories.pole_b_who: Positions commonly voiced by inflation hawks and cautious strategists.
evidence_left: The BLS reported +165,000 October jobs against a 65,000 consensus. Unemployment fell from 4.2% to 4.1%, and revisions added 84,000 to prior months (American Banker, TMGM).
Q3 growth was 3.4% (The Daily Upside). The Fed held rates at 3.75%–4% at its last meeting (American Banker).
evidence_right: The next CPI report is due Nov. 10. KuCoin, a single outlet, puts December hike odds near 80% and September inflation at 3.7%.
The S&P 500 had its biggest weekly loss since April 2025 (Bloomberg). Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the year (KuCoin).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from American Banker, Axios, CNBC, The Daily Upside, November 09, 2026.

stories.headline: Chargers Fall to 0-8 as Justin Herbert Is Sacked Eight Times
stories.dek: Houston's 44-22 win leaves Los Angeles as the NFL's only winless team and raises questions about Jim Harbaugh's offense.
pole_a_bullets: The line is the problem, not Herbert: he has been sacked 31 times in eight games, a pace of 66.
Harbaugh himself called the protection unacceptable, and the team benched right guard Cole Strange during the game.
Herbert was playing hurt and wanted to stay in, and Harbaugh pulled him with a finger injury.
The season is lost, so the Chargers should look to 2027 and the No. 1 pick.
pole_b_bullets: Harbaugh and offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel own an offense that went 34-37 straight drives without a touchdown, depending on the count.
Herbert has thrown an interception in all eight games, so not every failure traces to the line.
The Chargers have lost 11 straight dating to last season, tying a club record, which points beyond one position group.
Harbaugh says the offense can be fixed and the locker room must not fracture, so quitting on the season is premature.
stories.pole_a_who: Takes commonly voiced by fans and analysts who blame the offensive line and personnel.
stories.pole_b_who: Counter-takes commonly voiced by critics of the coaching staff and the offense's design.
evidence_left: Houston won 44-22 on Nov. 8. Herbert was sacked a career-high eight times and left in the fourth quarter with a left-hand finger injury. Harbaugh said it "could be a fracture" (LA Times via AOL, Yahoo Sports).
The Texans' C.J. Stroud threw for 384 yards (Houston Press). The Titans and Dolphins are 1-7 (Yahoo Sports).
evidence_right: The touchdown drought was 34 consecutive possessions per NFL insider Ari Meirov (via Yahoo Sports) and 37 per the Los Angeles Times (via AOL).
Herbert finished with 193 passing yards, one touchdown and one interception (Yahoo Sports).
stories.sources_line: Sourced from Yahoo Sports, Los Angeles Times via AOL, Houston Press, November 09, 2026.
